title: Plinko and Mines: Casino Originals Explained in Canada
excerpt: Plinko and Mines look nothing like slots, but the maths underneath is familiar. Here is how these casino originals work and what Canadian players should know.
author: Lisa Davids
bodyHtml:
Plinko and Mines have become two of the most recognisable casino originals available to Canadian players, and they arrived without any of the usual trappings of online gambling. There are no reels, no paylines, no bonus rounds and no theme. There is a grid or a pyramid, a bet amount, and a payout that changes as you make choices. That stripped-back presentation is exactly why they appeal to players who find modern slots cluttered — and exactly why it is worth understanding what is actually happening underneath.

This guide explains how both games work, how their maths is constructed, where the house edge lives, and how Canadian players should approach them without mistaking simplicity for favourable odds.

What casino originals actually are

Casino originals are in-house games built by an operator or a specialist studio rather than licensed from a traditional slots provider. They emerged from the crypto casino scene, where operators wanted games that were quick, visually minimal and easy to verify, and they have since spread to many Canadian-facing sites.

Three features define the category:

  • Player-adjustable risk: you choose the volatility rather than accepting whatever a slot was built with.
  • Instant rounds: results resolve in a second or two with no animation to sit through.
  • Transparent maths: most originals display the multiplier table and, on many crypto sites, a provably fair verification tool.

That last point is genuinely different from a traditional slot, where the RTP is disclosed but the individual outcome is not verifiable by the player. If you want the full picture of how that verification works, our crypto casino guide for Canadians covers the mechanics.

How Plinko works

Plinko drops a ball from the top of a triangular peg board. The ball bounces left or right at each row and lands in one of the slots along the bottom, each carrying a multiplier. Slots at the outer edges pay the most; slots in the centre pay the least, frequently less than your stake.

The binomial distribution behind it

If each bounce is an independent coin flip, the landing position follows a binomial distribution. The centre slots are overwhelmingly the most likely outcomes and the edges are rare. On a sixteen-row board, the extreme outer slots are hit a fraction of a percent of the time, which is why they can carry multipliers in the hundreds or thousands while the game still holds an edge.

This is the crucial insight: Plinko is not a game of skill or physics. The distribution is fixed, and the multipliers are calibrated against it to produce a target return. Watching where previous balls landed tells you nothing about where the next one will land.

Risk settings and row counts

Most Plinko implementations let you choose a risk level (low, medium, high) and a number of rows (typically eight to sixteen). These do not change the house edge in any meaningful way. What they change is the shape of your results.

  • Low risk: most drops return close to your stake, with small wins and small losses. Bankroll declines slowly and predictably.
  • High risk: centre slots return a small fraction of your stake, so most drops lose heavily, but edge hits pay large multiples.
  • More rows: a wider spread of outcomes and higher maximum multipliers, with a correspondingly harsher centre.

The parallel to slots is exact. Choosing high-risk Plinko is the same decision as choosing a high-volatility slot, a subject we cover in more depth in our online slots guide.

How Mines works

Mines presents a grid, commonly five by five, containing a number of hidden bombs that you select before the round begins. You reveal tiles one at a time. Every safe tile increases your multiplier. Hitting a bomb ends the round and loses the stake. At any point you can cash out and bank the current multiplier.

The maths of each click

The probability of a safe reveal is simply the number of remaining safe tiles divided by the number of remaining hidden tiles. With three bombs on a twenty-five tile grid, the first click is safe 88% of the time. By the tenth successful click, the odds on each subsequent tile have worsened considerably, because the bombs make up a larger share of what is left.

The multiplier climbs to compensate, but it climbs at a rate set by the operator, and that rate embeds the house edge. Crucially, the expected value of clicking one more tile is negative at every single stage — the same as it is on the first click. There is no point in a Mines round where continuing becomes mathematically advantageous.

Choosing your bomb count

More bombs means a steeper multiplier curve and a much shorter expected run. Fewer bombs means slow, grinding gains that require many clicks to become meaningful. Again, this is a volatility dial, not an edge dial. A one-bomb game and a twenty-bomb game return roughly the same percentage over the long run, they just get there by completely different paths.

Where the house edge lives

Published return figures for well-built originals often sit in the 97% to 99% range, which compares favourably with most slots. That number is real, but it comes with an important caveat: round speed.

A slot spin takes three to five seconds with animation. A Plinko drop or a Mines click takes well under a second, and both games support auto-play. A 1% house edge applied to five hundred rounds per hour produces far more theoretical loss than a 4% edge applied to four hundred spins. Low house edge plus high speed is not the bargain it appears to be — it simply changes where the cost shows up.

Canadian players who are used to comparing RTP percentages across games should add a second column to that comparison: expected rounds per hour. Our overview of the most searched casino games in Canada shows how differently these formats sit alongside traditional titles.

Practical advice for Canadian players

A few habits keep originals in the entertainment column where they belong:

  • Set a session budget before you open the game, not after a losing streak.
  • Use the casino's own deposit and loss limits rather than relying on willpower against a one-second round.
  • Avoid auto-play entirely if you are new to the format. It removes the natural pause that lets you notice how much you have staked.
  • Ignore progression systems. Doubling after a loss fails on Plinko and Mines for the same reason it fails on roulette: the game has no memory and the table has a maximum.
  • Verify the provably fair seed if the site offers it, at least once, so you know the tool works.

It is also worth checking whether originals count toward bonus wagering. Many Canadian-facing casinos weight them at a low percentage or exclude them entirely, which catches out players who assume all games contribute equally. The bottom line

Plinko and Mines are honest games in the sense that they show you their maths. What they do not show you is the effect of speed, and that is where most of the real cost sits. Treat the risk sliders as volatility settings rather than strategy, understand that no click or drop is ever a positive-expectation decision, and cap both your budget and your round count before you start.
